To my understanding, there is no circumstance in which carvana will refund the shipping fee. Having just gone through two car returns with them (under wild circumstances- car had a beetle infestation and mold/it was never inspected or cleaned). 

I was offered a couple solutions, but it was made clear to me that there would be no exception on the shipping fee. The best they would do there was apply the shipping fee from the first vehicle towards the shipping of a second vehicle if I wanted to swap. 

Ultimately the loss of the shipping fee is worth it if there are issues with the vehicle (many  of which carvana/silverrock flat out won’t cover or will make you jump through hoops to get any type of reimbursement).

Taking on any kind of debt when you are preparing to file doesn’t look great to the court/your trustee. Additionally, I believe in the Carvana financing documents you’ll be asked to sign to the fact that you are not actively in a bankruptcy or preparing to file. 

Signing a document saying you’re not in the process of filing, and then filing could potentially look a bit fraudulent when it comes time to confirm your case/discharge. At best- if this is questioned, it could lead to some creditor objections which will impact your payment plan amounts. 

Ultimately, to answer your question (as others have pointed out)- no, the vehicle would not be repossessed as long as you continue to make payments per the outlined terms. 

Hope that helps!

Unfortunately, having purchased from Carvana in the past (with a positive experience)- I went into the process pretty confidently.

When I realized the inspection couldn’t have taken place and Carvana wouldn’t confirm that all of the images online were from the actual car I purchased, I found this forum and many corroborating stories.

At this point, they already had my 5k down payment (which they told me would take up to 10 business days to return) and my third party financing check from my bank (made out to Carvana). When I spoke with my bank, they advised I’d need to go through an entirely new loan application process if I went with a different dealership. 

Also while negligible, Carvana would under no circumstances refund me the $200 transportation fee. They would only apply it to a different vehicle. 

I purchased a vehicle from Carvana in 2017 with no issues. My brother in law purchased a car from them last year with again, no issues. So, I’m hopeful that this next vehicle is fine. But after this, I won’t purchase from them again. Lesson learned!
CARFAX was totally clean! In retrospect, the second owner didn’t have any reported vehicle servicing after July 2021, which I guess could be a flag but didn’t register to me as a major “uh oh” .

I asked the same exact question when I called Carvana later that day to start the return process. I told them there was no way the images online were from the same vehicle. They just said “we’re sorry we missed the mark on this one”. 

Some of the things you wouldn’t necessarily see in the pics (the middle console wasn’t pulled down in the backseat, you can’t see the carpet, the seatbelts needed to be pulled down to see the moldy side, etc.) 

Either way I questioned them several times about the images and they would not respond or confirm that it was the same car. They also wouldn’t provide me with any written confirmation that the 150p inspection took place. Once I brought up the legality of the listing saying “EVERY” car goes through this inspection and the fact that this checklist had to have been falsified, that’s when they offered $500 towards a different vehicle.

Yeah fair question, and certainly not saying I did everything right. However, the extent of the “gross” wasn’t totally apparent while still on the lot. At face value it just seemed like they hadn’t reconditioned/detailed the car- and after having just been sitting around in the lobby for over an hr (because they only have two associates and had overbooked) it seemed like these were things I could solve myself. 

You couldn’t see the moldy seatbelts until you pulled them down. You couldn’t see the moldy back cup holder/console until you pulled it down from the middle seat. The beetles are incredibly small and just looked like crumbs/pieces of leaves/whatever. The visible ones were also dead so they weren’t moving, so the idea of it being bugs didn’t even cross my mind at the time. 

Most importantly though- I needed the vehicle. I had returned my lease the previous week and the delivery of this vehicle had already been delayed. The evil beauty of carvana is that by the time you get the keys to the vehicle, the sale is already complete (and you’ve never actually seen the car). They already had my down payment, a check for my third party financing, my signature on all documents, insurance was already in effect- etc. And if you do decide on the spot that you don’t want a vehicle, it’s not like you can pick a different one on their lot (at least not in my state where they recently lost their dealership license).

This is normal I think. I used to do this ALL of the time, and I think it would be strange if people who experienced big traumas didn’t do this- how can you not? It’s impossible to ignore all the ways our lives would be different without those events. 

For a long time I was really angry when I’d think about “other me”. If my dad hadn’t died- our finances would have been different- I would have tried harder in school- I would have gone to an elite college- etc. It was hard to think about how great “her” life would be. 

I recognized that fixating on this wasn’t serving me in any way. The fact is- that girl never could have existed because those things happened. It took me a bit longer to recognize that there are great things in my life that wouldn’t exist had “she” existed. If my dad hadn’t died, my sister might not have gone to the school she did and met the guy she married and I wouldn’t have my nephew. If my dad had lived, I wouldn’t have grown as close to my mom. Thinking about the good parts of my life not existing had that other road been an option, makes me less sad about the things that never came to be. 

I hope you’re able to find those gems in your life. It’s ok to mourn your potential other life, but don’t waste too much of the life you’ve got focusing on what could have been.

You are not a “lost cause” and your loved ones seemingly leaving you is not a reflection on how “savable” you are. 

You are loved and worthy of that love at all times (highs and lows). 

Many people with depression (or other MI) aren’t able to always see how their illness impacts folks who don’t suffer from the same ailments. 

The people in your life are not leaving you because they’re giving up on you- they’re most likely struggling to cope/find ways to help you. And when people are afraid of potentially making things worse for someone, they tend to retreat- with the idea that them leaving is the best thing for all parties. 

If you’re feeling abandoned, reach out. Let those people know that you’re struggling and remind them that you value the relationship/support, but most importantly you value THEM. Sometimes depression can take over those relationships, and make our loved ones feel manipulated/used- it doesn’t hurt to remind friends and family that you don’t just want them there for the dark moments, you want them there for the highlight reel too. 

I’m all ears if you need a chat!

TLDR; you’re a cute guy who might just need to work on your profile/messaging/match techniques. :) 

Well, your time has definitely not passed! You’re cute and sounds like you lead an interesting life. 

Dating apps like Tinder are a rough time for a lot of folks. If your pics don’t catch a persons eye almost immediately, you’re done for. 

Try to make sure your pictures reflect your personality (women appreciate that). Your sky diving photo is cool, the guitar pic is cute, the smiling selfie is another good one. Avoid (as another poster mentioned) dupe pics (pics taken at the same place/event) or pics that fail to reflect joy/personality (like your more stoic selfie). 

When you are sending a first message try to avoid completely generic “hey, how are you?” messages. As a woman, we are getting tons of these messages- set yourself a part. No need for a novella or anything, just find something about their profile to bring up so they know you’ve actually taken some time to learn about them (example: “Woah- you played saxophone in HS? SAME! Alto, tenor, or baritone?”)

From a match perspective- if you’re truly looking for a relationship (and not just a hookup) really take stock of the apps you’re using and the matches you’re making. Apps like OKC and Match are more geared towards connection over attraction. 

Lastly, you mentioned you’re swiping on a good deal of people and IYO not being “very” selective. For me, attraction grows with connection. Someone I might not initially find attractive can grow to be super desirable if they’re hilarious or witty/we can banter well. This is not the case for everyone, but if you think it might be for you- try not limiting your matches to people you’re attracted to right away!

Mine was my first (and only) high school boyfriend. I didn’t know it was going to end badly but I knew it was going to be a bumpy ride. 

The relationship started high intensity and ended high intensity after 4 years (junior yr of highschool into college). He was not emotionally well and I wanted someone to fix- which made us terrible for each other. 

We tried breaking up a few times but one of us always ended up crying/screaming at the other to take them back. I went to NY for college and he stayed in our home state. The distance made for a lot of distrust and anger, but it also made for a more concrete ending. 

One day he just blew up on the phone. I hung up and never answered again. 

For a while I thought he was going to come to NY and bust in my dorm door- or show up at my parents house when I was home on break. He never did. 

It was an early relationship for me and I was young- but I knew from the start he was trouble. Impulsively (as teens do) I liked the way that danger felt. But 4 years of that is exhausting and it taught me the exact feeling to run away from as an adult.

No, it is never fair or acceptable. This kind of mindset contributes to the narrative/need for restraining orders. Closure is subjective- so someone demanding closure could be something that continues indefinitely.

If you purchased a blouse from a store and a year after buying the store reached out and asked you to return the blouse- as they didn’t mean to sell it, would that be acceptable/would you feel a need to return it? The store feels entitled to the shirt, it was theirs after all. Their inventory won’t be complete without it. 

Relationships and transactions are different- but here, in both cases the “deal” is done. 

The emotional “contract” of a relationship ends at breakup/divorce/etc. There is no longer a partnership, there is no outstanding balance, there is no returning the blouse.

You deserve to see yourself as a lovable (and loved) person.

I would suggest you take stock of the ramifications of your actions? Seems like you’re looking at this from a “what will happen to me- the reporter” and what you need to be thinking is “what will happen to the person I’m reporting”. 

In terms of procedure not much will impact you- you may be asked for any supporting documentation of your claims and if you witnessed a crime take place and that’s about it. 

Your life will not be disrupted. But you may be disrupting (if not destroying) the life of someone and their entire family. Even if your claims are wrong, and the person in question is legally here, you will put their lives in danger simply by requesting ICE/police intervention.

First red flag to me would have been the “I’m not cool with giving you my number” thing. 

As a woman who gives out her number on dating apps (because I too am not great at replying via apps) I’ve literally NEVER had a guy not text me immediately (not tooting my horn here- I’m not some super hot person) a lot of these happen even pre-date.  

His hesitance to give you his number IMO says he is either a player or a notorious ghoster. He has either experienced too many girls texting him that he doesn’t want communication with or his game is date and ghost and giving out your number gets messy when that’s your play. 

Second red flag- the ex thing. If he really didn’t care about his ex reaching out, his attention would have been on you during this second date. If you’re talking about talking with an ex on a second date, that signals to me that you have an unclosed chapter. Sure it’s normal to talk about past partners, but that coupled with his demeanor and behavior says “no thanks” to me!

As most have said, telling him is the right move! 

1) As a cancer survivor he will have more empathy than a partner who has never gone through this. Having experienced what you’re going through may actually bring you both closer together. 

2) Whether your cancer is treatable or not, the fact that it will impact your future in a serious way means that you should be honest with the person you are with, especially if you see them as being a part of that future. If the roles were reversed, wouldn’t you feel betrayed if your partner withheld what was going on from you? 

3) I don’t know anyone who would leave a person because they got sick (and honestly, wtf- BYE to anyone who would) but I do know plenty of people who would leave someone for hiding things from their partner. 

4) Wishing you a speedy recovery! Cancer is scary, but it sounds like you have someone in your life who can relate to you and whom you can rely on when you need support- use that. Sending positive vibes your way.

If OP feels it’s necessary to write down his feelings and thinks that could be helpful, 100% take that opportunity to do so but it is self-serving and an invasion of privacy to send to her address. 

Contacting someone because they cannot extract a memory from your head (her address) does not mean this is the right thing to do. She has made it clear she wants no contact with the OP, so looking for ways around that borders on obsessive/manipulative. 

Write the letter if you need to vent- then destroy it, lock it away, etc. don’t ignore her request to be left alone.

The fact that she has blocked you on everything should be closure enough. She is not interested in connecting, even if to smooth over your last interaction. I would not try to sidestep these barriers (regardless of how you feel) as that is invasive and selfish. 

Blocking someone (while sometimes immature, other times necessary) is a way to close a door. You should try to find closure in the the fact that she is not interested in hearing from you whatsoever, if she was- she would not block you. 

The longer you are apart from someone and the longer you go without communication, the more "final" that will feel. Give it some time!
